subject: treasureChest
pitch: A pirate's treasure chest with its lid thrown open. Weathered dark wood planks bound with rusty iron straps and studs, a heavy padlock hanging loose, and spilling out of it: gold coins, a pearl necklace, a jewelled goblet and a few red and green gems. A small skull-and-crossbones is carved on the front.
reasoning:
I'm planning the chest structure with a root "base" joint and a separate "lid" joint at the back hinge so the lid can be posed open or closed.

Working out dimensions in meters: a wood box body roughly 0.9m wide, 0.42m tall, 0.56m deep, with a wood grain paint for weathered planks, plus iron straps and stud spheres for hardware, and a curved lid box attached to the hinge joint.

I'm placing the lid hinge joint at the back top edge and working through the rotation math so the lid swings open and upward around the X axis rather than collapsing downward, deciding it's simpler to just build the lid geometry directly in its open world position using the joint's local coordinates rather than fighting the rotation math.

Since the lid joint is rigid with identity orientation anyway, I'll skip posing and just place the lid box directly with the computed rotation, sizing it roughly 0.9 x 0.12 x 0.56. For the interior, I'll add a dark inner board slightly below the rim, visible when the lid is open.

Then I'm scattering a treasure pile: dozens of small flat cylindrical coins tossed across the interior and over the front rim, plus a pearl necklace made of small spheres draped in an arc over them, and a goblet shaped with a lathe profile.

I'm giving the goblet a solid gold color and embedding small red and green gem spheres along its stem and rim, with the coins colored a matching gold tone. For the front decoration, I'm considering a simple skull-and-crossbones motif built from spheres rather than a complex decal.

Now I'm placing the skull using an off-white sphere with a jaw box and dark eye sockets, and crossing two thin capsule "bones" behind it in a bone-colored tone, positioned near the front face. I'm also working out where the padlock should hang loosely from a hasp plate mounted on the body's front face, since the lid is open and the lock needs to dangle below its shackle rather than sit flush.

For the padlock itself, I'm sizing a small box for the body and attaching a half-torus shackle above it, oriented so the arc faces outward and is visible from the front. Then I'm laying out iron reinforcement straps as thin boxes across the front and top surfaces of the trunk to give it that banded, metal-fitted look.

I'm placing vertical straps on the front, back, and sides with small sphere studs along them, plus faint horizontal seam lines to suggest wooden planks making up the body. Below that I'm scattering a pile of coins using randomized positions and tilts—some heaped on top with radial falloff, others spilled flat onto the floor in front—using thin cylinders to represent each coin.

I'm adding small gem spheres and a pearl necklace scattered over the coin pile, plus a goblet resting on top near the edge. For materials, I'm building layered wood paints combining grain and mottle textures in dark weathered browns for both the chest body and lid, and starting on a rusted iron color for the straps.

Now I'm setting up the joint structure: a root "base" joint at the origin and a "lid" joint positioned at the back edge for the hinge, aligning the hinge axis along local X. I'm deciding to explicitly assign parts to their bones ("base" or "lid") rather than relying on automatic nearest-joint detection, since with only two joints that could misassign lid parts.

For the geometry, I'm placing the body as a box roughly 0.9 by 0.42 by 0.56 centered above the base, and the lid as a similarly-sized box rotated about -100° on X to swing open, painted as wood. I'm now working out how to attach iron strap details onto the lid's rotated surface, since the straps need to follow the lid's tilted local frame rather than world coordinates.

Rather than manually rotating child geometry, I realize I should define a region anchored at the lid's center with the same quaternion rotation, so parts placed inside it inherit the local orientation automatically. I'm checking how the lid's local axes map after the -100° X rotation to make sure the strap placement and the lid's outward-facing normal actually point the right way once rotated.

Placing straps on the lid slightly above its top surface, and setting up the region/bone options so straps inherit the lid's or base's bone weighting correctly. Now I'm positioning body straps along the front face of the base box, matching their depth to sit flush against it.

Working out horizontal and side straps for the body, then placing decorative studs at strap intersections across the front face using a grid of x positions and two y rows.

Now I'm designing a skull emblem centered on the front plate with scaled sphere geometry for the cranium, a jawbone box, dark recessed eye sockets, and crossbones positioned diagonally behind the skull near the lower straps.

I'm figuring out where to hang the padlock so it doesn't collide with the strap band or studs, settling on a hasp plate near the front-right top edge with the lock body tilted slightly for a loose, hanging look and a shackle arcing above it.

Settling on body center 0.3325 with the shackle's upper-arc torus meeting the box top edge cleanly. I'm defining the padlock box geometry, iron paint mottle texture, and gold solid color, then moving to arrange pearls along a draped arc for the necklace.

Now I'm figuring out the goblet's lathe profile — radius points along the stem and cup walls — trying to decide whether to cap the top solid or leave the cup open, plus placing small octahedron gems around the pile and goblet rim.

I solve the parametric equations and confirm the inner and outer wall segments don't intersect, so the cup geometry is valid. Now I'm setting the goblet's gold color and figuring out gem placement on the cup body, positioning the goblet relative to the pile of coins it sits in.

Then I work out the chest structure: building it as separate floor and wall boxes to keep the interior hollow so coins can fill it, rather than a solid box. I plan the coin heap using a radial falloff function for height based on distance from center, plus some coins spilling onto the floor outside the chest with random tilts and rotations for a tossed look.

For the lid, I work through the hinge geometry and rotation math to position the lid box and its iron straps correctly relative to the hinge joint, then move to decorating the front and back walls with iron straps, horizontal bands, and brass studs, placing a skull-and-crossbones motif on the front panel using bone-colored spheres, and defining wood and iron paint textures using grain and mottle functions along with the gold, pearl, red, green, and dark color palette. I'm writing the chest-building code...

Then I add a hanging padlock assembly with a hasp plate, torus shackle, and lock body positioned on the front panel, define the lid region with its hinge rotation and attach wood and iron straps to it, and scatter a pile of gold coins, pearls, and gems across the chest interior using a heap-height function so objects naturally follow the mound shape, plus a lathed goblet with inset gems sitting atop the coin pile. I'm writing the full scene-building function...
